\chapter{Weather}
\label{ch:fr-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about the weather in French — quel temps fait-il, il fait chaud, il fait froid, il pleut.}

Use le temps in both its senses, build the weather with faire (il fait chaud / il fait froid), and say il pleut with the Latin pl- cluster French kept intact. The chapter's only lesson, so the payoff covers everything it introduces.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[le temps, il pleut]{le temps, il pleut — the same Latin word, a different fate for \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C21-le-temps}



\begin{quote}
You've seen Spanish's \emph{tiempo} mean both \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} at once, from Latin \emph{tempus}. French has the exact same word, the exact same double meaning — because this widening happened within Latin itself, before French and Spanish went their separate ways.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words: le temps — time and weather}
\textbf{le temps} = both \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{time}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — from Latin \textbf{tempus}, same as Spanish's \emph{tiempo} (English kept only the \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} half: \textbf{temporal, tempo}). So \textbf{quel temps fait-il ?} (\textquotedblleft{}what's the weather like?\textquotedblright{}) is literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what time does it make}?\textquotedblright{} — the identical construction inside Spanish's \emph{¿qué tiempo hace?}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: il fait chaud / il fait froid}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Il fait chaud.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's hot.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{makes} hot.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Il fait froid.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's cold.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{makes} cold.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same \emph{hacer}-style periphrasis as Spanish, just with French's own \textbf{faire} (\textquotedblleft{}to make/do\textquotedblright{}).
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Il pleut.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — from \textbf{pleuvoir} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pluere}, \textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{same} Latin verb behind Spanish's \emph{llueve}. But here's the honest difference: Spanish underwent the \textbf{pl- $\to$ ll-} shift (\emph{pluere} $\to$ \emph{llover}), while French kept the \textbf{pl-} cluster fully intact — \emph{pleuvoir} still visibly starts with \emph{pl-}, just like the Latin original. So the same Latin verb took two different sound-change paths in its two daughters: one eroded the cluster, one preserved it.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le temps\textquotedblright{} — time, or weather, depending on context
  \item \textquotedblleft{}il fait chaud. il fait froid.\textquotedblright{} — it's hot/cold
  \item \textquotedblleft{}il pleut\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, pl- kept intact from Latin
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things does \textbf{le temps} mean, and where does this polysemy come from? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Time\textquotedblright{}} and \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{}} — from Latin \emph{tempus}, already double-sensed before French/Spanish split apart.) Does French's \emph{il pleut} show the same \emph{pl- $\to$ ll-} shift as Spanish's \emph{llueve}? (\textbf{No} — French kept the \emph{pl-} cluster intact; only Spanish underwent that shift.)
\end{tcolorbox}
